props.title: The Killers
props.initialSlug: Hit men investigate why their target didn't run

sections.content: The Killers represents a fascinating evolution from its 1946 noir predecessor, both based on Hemingway's short story. Don Siegel's neon-bright, hard-edged version transforms the material into a brutal crime thriller that influenced generations of filmmakers. The film marked Ronald Reagan's last screen appearance - and his only villain role - while Lee Marvin and Angie Dickinson deliver career-defining performances. Siegel's version abandons the shadowy noir aesthetics for harsh sunlight and stark violence, presaging the shift toward more explicit crime films like Point Blank (1967) and Dirty Harry (1971).

sections.content: The film's influence on crime cinema can't be overstated. Its cold-blooded opening sequence directly inspired Pulp Fiction (1994), while its narrative structure - using multiple perspectives to piece together a crime - became a template for films like The Killing (1956) and Reservoir Dogs (1992). Siegel's economical direction and unflinching violence established a new template for American crime films, moving away from film noir's expressionist shadows toward something more documentarian and brutal.

The 1964 version also marked a crucial shift in how Hollywood depicted criminal violence. While the 1946 version relied on suggestion and shadow, Siegel's adaptation features stark, matter-of-fact brutality that would become standard in films like Bonnie and Clyde (1967) and The Wild Bunch (1969). The film's opening hit sequence - two killers methodically executing their target - remains shocking even today. SUBHEAD: The Reagan Factor

sections.content: Ronald Reagan's performance as villainous crime boss Jack Browning represents a fascinating footnote in cinema history. As his final film role before entering politics, it offers a stark contrast to his earlier good-guy image. The casting choice seems almost prophetic - The Dead Zone (1983) would later cast its own sinister politician, while films like Secret Honor (1984) and Nixon (1995) would continue exploring the intersection of crime and politics through the lens of the presidency.
